articles.title: What the election results could mean for gas prices, groceries, and health insurance
articles.summary: What the midterm elections could mean for gas prices, groceries, health insurance, and housing costs, and how to budget while Congress changes hands.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

The midterm election put Democrats in charge of both the House and Senate, reshaping Washington against a backdrop of rising inflation, tariffs, and conflict in the Middle East.

Democrats will take over as the majority when the new Congress is sworn in in January. The party's leaders have been critical of Trump policies as the cost of living rises in the U.S. Here's a look at the issues they will try to solve, and how their efforts could affect Americans' finances.

In January of 2026, the national average retail gas price was $2.81 per gallon. The U.S. and Israel initiated the conflict with Iran at the end of February. By April, gas prices had increased to $4.10. The average has remained above $4 per gallon since then, except in July. October's average was $4.31, down from $4.36 in September.

The elevated prices at the pump are largely driven by the war in Iran. The conflict has disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, a primary oil shipping route, creating a supply shock that has reverberated around the world.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has said his party will fight to end the Iran war. An end to the conflict may eventually reduce gas prices, but it depends on what happens in the Strait of Hormuz. Jeffries has also called on the Trump administration to wind down the war effort this year.

These are the steps Congress can take on the war itself and gas prices:

End funding for the Iran war. The Senate and the House approve new funding requests for the war. Once the new Congress is sworn in, the Democrats can deny those requests.

Pass a resolution to end the war. Congress can pass a resolution with a Democratic majority, but the president can veto it. The Democrats will not have the two-thirds majority required to override a presidential veto.

Suspend the federal gas tax and the federal diesel tax. The federal government taxes gas at $0.184 per gallon and diesel at $0.244 per gallon. Several federal lawmakers and President Trump have expressed support for pausing both taxes, so this could be a bipartisan effort.

A suspension of the federal gas and diesel taxes is the quickest lever, but the potential benefit would offset only a fraction of the increases drivers have absorbed this year.

Grocery and everyday prices: Tariffs and diesel cost effects remain

General inflation, according to the Consumer Price Index , has remained above 3% since March. The September inflation reading was 3.7%, an increase from the prior month's rate of 3.4%. Prior to this year, inflation had not ticked above 3% since May of 2024.

Food prices have not risen as quickly. The inflation rate on groceries was 1.8% in September, but has been as high as 2.9% this year.

Economists cite the war in Iran as a primary driver. Elevated diesel costs can put upward pressure on food and everyday prices by increasing manufacturing and transportation costs.

Tariffs are also a factor. While importers pay tariffs directly, they often pass these costs along to consumers in the form of higher prices.

What Democrats can do about grocery prices

Realistically, Democrats aren't likely to lower food prices, but they can work to slow the pace of inflation, which means prices won't rise as quickly. But most of the factors affecting food prices are outside of Congress' control, including climate, crop performance, labor, and other costs.

Tariffs are the exception. Repealing tariffs on imported foods or packaging materials could lead to price reductions for certain products. However, the path to a full tariff repeal is complicated. A Democratic Congress can pass bills to roll back the levies still in force, but President Trump can veto them.

Other efforts to pause the diesel tax or end the war in Iran won't immediately lower grocery prices.

Health insurance: Open enrollment is here

Enhanced Affordable Care Act income-based tax credits, called PTCs, that made healthcare more affordable for qualifying Americans expired at the end of 2025. Democrats and Republicans couldn't agree on the future of the tax credits, and the disagreement led to an extended government shutdown last year.

Democrats have vowed to restore PTCs and Medicaid funding that Republicans cut. Jeffries has defined both moves as high-priority items, alongside the repeal of Trump's tariffs.

What Democrats can do about healthcare costs

Democrats have two avenues for achieving their healthcare goals, and neither is certain or immediate:

As the minority party, they can demand healthcare changes in the next government funding bill — which will replace the current funding bill that runs out on December 11, 2026. This tactic didn't work last year and could result in a government shutdown.

Alternatively, they can wait until January, when they're sworn in as the majority, to pass new bills. President Trump will still have veto power, however.

In most states, open enrollment for individual and family ACA marketplace plans runs from Nov. 1 to Jan. 15, but Dec. 15 is the last date to enroll for coverage starting Jan. 1. Medicare open enrollment runs from Oct. 15 through Dec. 7.

Relief on healthcare costs isn't likely in the short term.

The national average fixed rate on a 30-year mortgage has been rising since July, peaking in October at 7.4%. Like gas prices, mortgage rates began declining in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections. The last calculated average is 7.18% as of Nov. 5.

The CPI shelter measure, which lags market rents by six to 12 months, has been rising at an annual rate of 3% or more throughout 2026. For context, this measure of housing inflation was 8.2% in March of 2023 and has been slowly declining since.

What Democrats can do about mortgage rates and rents

Mortgage rates are driven by Treasury yields , inflation expectations, and macroeconomic factors. Rents move primarily with supply and demand.

Congress doesn't have direct influence in any of these areas. Their likely playbook would involve legislation to promote housing supply, assist with rents or home down payments, or reduce the cost of mortgage insurance. Any new programs would be subject to presidential veto and, if enacted, would deliver gradual results at best.

The midterm election results may feel like a big win for those who voted for Democrats, but cost-of-living trends don't change overnight. Bills take time to pass, and their economic effects are usually gradual. With that in mind, it's wise to stay conservative financially. Here are some moves to consider.

Keep budgeting. Plan for gas and food prices to remain elevated. A wind-down of the conflict in the Middle East should lead to lower gas prices, but the timing is uncertain. Be prepared for high gas prices as the new normal. That way, it'll feel like a bonus when prices at the pump start to moderate.

Secure healthcare coverage. Don't miss open enrollment waiting for cheaper options. There aren't likely to be any big changes in healthcare until next year.

Evaluate refinancing and new mortgage options carefully. Mortgage rates often follow 10-year Treasury yields. And Treasury yields tend to decline after midterm elections, according to Swiss bank and asset manager Lombard Odier. While mortgage rates may decline over the next few months, economic conditions remain unpredictable. So, exercise caution on refinancing or homebuying decisions. Weigh refinancing opportunities on the break-even timeline and evaluate new mortgages on affordability.

Add to an emergency fund. Beefing up emergency savings provides financial flexibility and helps keep credit card debt in check. Start the habit now and increase your savings deposits if lower gas prices create more breathing room in the budget.

Don't change an investing approach. According to JPMorgan, the S&P 500 has gained in the year following every midterm election since 1950. The average gain has been about 15%. The lesson? Don't change an investing approach in response to the midterm election results. If the state of a retirement account still raises concern, revisit the asset mix and ensure it aligns with the set investment timeline and risk tolerance.

In January, the balance of power in Washington will change. Democrats will control Congress, alongside a president who can veto their legislative efforts. The cost-of-living pressures aren't likely to ease quickly — so budget as if they're here to stay.

articles.title: Nvidia faces a more hostile Washington

articles.body:
CEO Jensen Huang's close relationship with President Trump is unlikely to inoculate the company from an increasingly hostile Washington, as Democrats prepare to take over regulatory committees and key Republicans look to impose stronger high tech export controls.

Plus, three Republican House members recently requested Huang appear in a private briefing on whether he was the target of a Chinese spy . Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo did not directly answer whether Huang would attend the briefing, telling Semafor in a statement: "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know. We often receive updates from the U.S. government regarding parties and entities of concern and always act accordingly."

In the lame duck, a must-pass defense bill could include export control measures that would further restrict chip sales to China. (It could pass even more easily next year.) Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., likely the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has long wanted Huang to testify before Congress on Nvidia's tranche of deals with other tech companies, and chip sales to China.

Trump will have to decide if protecting Huang's interest is more important than working with Congress on this issue as the debate over AI shifts.

articles.title: Elizabeth Warren will take over the Senate Banking Committee next year. Expect hearings.
articles.summary: Warren will use the committee's investigative powers to hold hearings and investigations into executive branch ethics and corporate practices, aiming to hold...
articles.body:
Democratic firebrand Elizabeth Warren, a consumer advocate known for her fierce battles over financial regulations, will take the gavel in January to become chair of the powerful Senate Banking Committee.

According to a source familiar with her plans, the Massachusetts senator intends to use her expanded platform to advance legislation to tackle populist affordability issues with a focus on housing.

The person familiar with her plans says Warren will use the committee's investigative powers to hold hearings and launch investigations into executive branch ethics and corporate practices, aiming to hold President Trump, the administration, Wall Street, and Big Tech accountable for economic decisions she views as having driven up costs for consumers.

Warren is also expected to take steps to shield the Federal Reserve from White House overreach . Any future nominee for the Fed will have to go through her committee. Earlier this year, she rallied Democrats to oppose Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's confirmation before the banking committee, stalling his eventual confirmation.

Wall Street is likely to be another of Warren's targets. Before Republicans regained control of Congress, Democrats would have the chief executives of big banks testify before the Senate Banking and House Financial Services committees once a year. The banking industry can expect a return to that practice.

Stephen Biggar, who covers the financial sector for Argus Research, says hearings will offer more transparency, but won't be accompanied by meaningful rulemaking. Biggar expects increased oversight, potentially more consumer protections, and actions to limit banks' market share size, such as blocking mergers.

He added that there are concerns that the deregulation efforts and lower capital requirements for banks championed by Republicans are now at risk.

James Angel, an associate professor at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, said he thinks the hearings will accomplish two things: producing information and sound bites that will get people to pay attention and galvanize public opinion. Second, Angel says they will serve as a deterrent for people in power.

"If people will be held under oath and there's a prospect of perjury, that will deter people from doing 'Trumpier' things," Angel said in an interview.

Angel also noted that any Trump appointee who has to be confirmed by Warren's committee will need to withstand bipartisan scrutiny and thus is more likely to be a moderate.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Public sector oil marketing companies (OMCs) on Friday hit back at Congress-led Karnataka govt's claims that petrol tested by labs authorised
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Public sector oil marketing companies (OMCs) on Friday hit back at Congress-led Karnataka govt's claims that petrol tested by labs authorised by it had found ethanol content exceeding the prescribed 20% limit, and said the findings were not supported by tests conducted under statutory and technical procedures.Karnataka food, civil supplies and legal metrology minister Rizwan Arshad had claimed that tests conducted by its authorised laboratories on petrol samples from across the state were "alarming", showing ethanol content as high as 31.2%.Late in the evening, rebutting the claims, the three oil retailers - Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation - questioned the sampling and testing methodology adopted during an Oct exercise by the state govt, arguing that the procedure did not follow the requirements laid down under the Motor Spirit and High Speed Diesel Control Order, 2005, and Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG), 2024. They said the samples were drawn without the participation of their representatives.Countering the state's findings, the fuel retailers said all 893 samples collected from OMC depots and retail outlets across 27 states and Union Territories under a quality monitoring exercise conducted by petroleum ministry's Centre for High Technology were found to contain ethanol within the prescribed 19-21% range."The 56 samples tested in Karnataka, covering different locations and all three OMCs, also met the specifications, recording ethanol content between 19% and 20%, with an average of 19.3%," the fuel retailers said.The fuel retailers sought complete sampling documentation, outlet-wise laboratory reports and details of the testing methodology from Karnataka govt, besides access to counterpart samples for independent testing at an authorised laboratory in the presence of state govt and company representatives.The companies said they were willing to cooperate with the state govt in a joint sampling and testing exercise in accordance with the prescribed procedures.Arshad earlier said laboratory findings from 14 of the 63 petrol bunks, which also included Nayara, Shell and MRPL facilities, besides the three state-run OMCs, showed a maximum of 31.2% and 30.5% ethanol blending in some IOCL and HPCL petrol bunks, respectively, which were way beyond the stipulated 20%. Blending at some BPCL, Nayara and Shell bunks were also found to be beyond the prescribed limit.Karnataka govt claimed that the samples were initially sent to IOCL and HPCL labs for testing. "However, these laboratories did not disclose the ethanol content in the fuel," it said, claiming this raised serious questions about the transparency of these oil marketing companies.You use AI every day. articles.title: Could the ‘blue tsunami’ jolt the US job market back to life?
articles.summary: The US labor market has been amazingly resilient in the face of a barrage of economic shocks.
articles.body: The US labor market has been amazingly resilient in the face of a barrage of economic shocks. The unemployment rate has been at or under 4.5% for a record-setting five years and Friday’s stronger-than-expected jobs report for October showed that employers are hiring at one of the fastest clips in the past three years. But the monthly snapshot also revealed some troubling trends: Americans’ average stint on unemployment is the longest it’s been in nearly five years; the bulk of the job gains remain relatively concentrated to few industries; and workers’ wages continue to fall further behind inflation. So, while the labor market may be stable, it has not been running on all cylinders: Its gears have been gummed up for quite some time. Economists have questioned how long the stasis could last, and what could cause it to break in one direction or the other. The “blue tsunami” has now entered the chat. What that means for the labor market’s trajectory remains to be seen – it’s still very early innings, and there are plenty of weightier factors already at play. But here are some of the areas economists are watching closely amid a reshaping of the political landscape: Nothing is changing overnight First things first, change takes time and policies have limitations. “Elections can shift the policy outlook, but they rarely change the labor market overnight,” said Cory Stahle, senior economist at online job marketplace Indeed. “The forces shaping hiring right now, from an aging workforce to AI adoption, were in place before the election and will still be there next year.” The labor market is undergoing some structural shifts. The labor force is shrinking because of an aging population, increased retirements from Baby Boomers, and a reduction in net immigration. Technological innovations, notably artificial intelligence, are transforming jobs, industries and the economy. To address the concerns of businesses wrestling with labor supply constraints, policies can be implemented to increase immigration or encourage more people to have children, but the effects of those don’t happen overnight, he said. If Americans are wanting to see quicker changes that impact their personal economies, that’s much more likely to come at the state level than at the national level, said Tyler Schipper, associate professor of economics at St. Thomas University in St. Paul, Minnesota. At the national level, Congress can only do so much by itself, and President Donald Trump still has veto power, Schipper said. At the state level, there’s more that can be done, he said, to address affordability concerns for businesses and the consumers that power the economy. But even those take time. “For instance, states can do a lot of work on transportation networks, and they can do a lot to make housing more affordable; but those are both investments that don’t see quick returns, even if they are investments that start right away in January,” he said. Silver lining of gridlock A divided federal government comes with some risks. “What we might see at the national level is more gridlock and a lot of budget negotiations that have the potential to lead to government shutdowns,” Schipper said. “So, I am not entirely sure that people get the quick wins maybe they were hoping for at the national level.” Gridlock also suggests that major policy changes may be limited. And that, in a way, could provide a dash of much-needed certainty. “One of the drags on hiring has been uncertainty – uncertainty around tariffs, uncertainty around energy prices,” said Gus Faucher, chief economist at PNC Financial Services. “We might see lower levels of uncertainty, and overall, that’s good news for the labor market.” Tariffs and war Sweeping tariffs on imports have been a signature economic policy for Trump, who has stated a desire to bolster America’s manufacturing industry and generate federal revenue. Manufacturing employment is showing some signs of life after a post-pandemic bout of job-shedding, including the loss of 113,000 jobs last year: Through October, the industry, which employs 12.7 million people, has added 101,000 jobs and has seen net gains for five months in a row. However, those higher import costs were passed through supply chains and consumers, adding upward pressure to inflation last year. As those effects started to fade early this year, the US and Israel’s strikes on Iran set off a monthslong war that caused an energy shock that sent gas prices – and inflation – higher, further compounding Americans’ yearslong affordability concerns. Goldman Sachs economists, in a note earlier this week, said they expect Democrats to use fiscal deadlines to seek limiting the war with Iran, roll back selected tariffs and reverse spending cuts enacted last year. It’s possible there could be enough bipartisan support in Congress to convince Trump to stop a trade war with a particular country, such as Canada, Schipper said. As for the Iran conflict, a War Powers Resolution might not be veto-proof. “Even if congressional pressure can help wrap up the war, a lot of the lingering effects that people are feeling, those don’t immediately go away,” he said. “The damage has been done, and that’s going to take quite a bit of time to resolve, even once the conflict has some kind of durable end.” Looming healthcare cuts The healthcare and social assistance sector, buoyed by some of the demographic shifts that are shrinking the labor force, has been responsible for the lion’s share of employment gains in recent years. That industry faces significant risks as a result of major cuts on Medicaid eligibility and funding set to take effect on January 1, 2027, said Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG. “We don’t know what’s going to happen if [Congress] gets a reconciliation package in the lame duck session or not,” Swonk said. “If they don’t, this is something that Democrats are going to want to try to get through themselves.” The cuts would create a big hole to fill for the state and local governments that administer the programs, she said. It could result in fewer programs and clinics as well as increased consolidation, negatively impacting jobs and services, she said. “It’s really hard on rural areas but also in lower-income areas as well,” she said. The AI elephant in the room While AI has the potential to reshape the economy and millions of jobs, the technology also has been met with much concern and fear from Americans – especially as it relates to their jobs and household finances. AI adoption has been a frequent reason cited in companies’ layoff plans in recent months, Challenger, Gray & Christmas data shows; however, those tend to overstate what’s actually happening in the labor market, PNC’s Faucher said. “AI, at least as of yet, has not been transformative for the labor market,” he said. Stricter regulations around AI and data centers aren’t likely to immediately occur at the federal level, according to the Goldman Sachs projections. The same can’t be said for the state level, their economists noted. “The states where Democrats are likely to further restrict data centers account for roughly 45% of planned US data center capacity, with Texas alone accounting for roughly 25%,” they wrote. “However, since data centers are low on the list of priorities for voters this election, we expect that the issue will fade somewhat in importance in the ensuing months and that these moratoria will not be long-lived if they are enacted.” Tuesday’s election results provide a check on AI companies and allow communities to have a greater say in who does and doesn’t want them, Schipper said. “It means that communities that might be more economically distressed have a better chance of winning some of those data AI center contracts, where it could actually have meaningful impacts in those communities,” he said. It’s possible that a slowing of AI-related developments could ease concerns that the rapid boom in investment would be followed by a bust, said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US. The slowing in AI-related spending also could also open up more non-tech investment, he said. “The boom in AI was crowding out both public and private-sector investment,” Brusuelas added. “The idea there’s going to be a slowing means there will be a redirection of capital into the real economy to meet legitimate needs of non-tech areas.” Still, as the markets’ volatility showed Thursday, risks remain that a prolonged correction in AI stocks could have big negative wealth effects that bleed into the larger economy. US consumer spending has been robust in part because of the wealth effects created by the strong stock market. Great expectations There are understated expectation effects from the midterm results, Schipper said. If people can properly set their expectations about how much a Democratic Congress can do on its own, those expectations could ultimately have an effect on the broader economy, he added. Consumer sentiment has been circling the drain for much of this year as a war-driven spike in gas prices and concerns about AI’s potential negative effects on the labor market have further compounded affordability concerns. “One of the things that’s been holding the economy back, not sending into a recession, but maybe holding it back, has been that people are generally pessimistic about both their current circumstances and the future,” he said. “People might feel slightly more positive if they see more of their politicians working for them, even if it’s not necessarily getting results.”

articles.title: Decline in gold price pushes jewellery sales on Dhanteras
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A dip in gold prices drew shoppers to jewellery stores on Dhanteras on Friday.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A dip in gold prices drew shoppers to jewellery stores on Dhanteras on Friday. Carmakers lined up thousands of festive deliveries, while televisions led demand at an electronics retailer.Senco Gold & Diamonds reported sales growth of more than 25% by value, with footfall up 10-12% from last year, CEO Suvankar Sen said.Kalyan Jewellers said its price for 22-carat gold fell Rs 235 a gram from Thursday to Rs 13,150 on Friday. Executive director Ramesh Kalyanaraman said footfall picked up, with shoppers favouring lighter pendants, bangles and chains, as well as smaller gold and silver coins. The chain saw more first-time buyers in cities such as Jaipur, Dehradun and Raipur."The dip in gold prices helped to boost demand, as many buyers who were waiting for a correction stepped in," said Paul Alukkas, managing director of Jos Alukkas.In Delhi's Madangir jewellery market, Ramavtar Soni, director of Prabhu Dayal & Sons Jewellers, said demand for gold and silver coins has risen, with shoppers buying them as symbols of prosperity on Dhanteras. Rama Krishna Jewellers added that the recent price dip had encouraged purchases and that shoppers continued to see gold as a store of value.Giva founder and CEO Ishendra Agarwal said 9-carat jewellery, introduced four months ago, accounted for about a quarter of revenue for its gold and lab-grown diamond business."Buying patterns are evolving, with consumers increasingly gravitating towards lightweight, versatile designs that offer value without compromising on aesthetics or aspiration," said Kirit Bhansali, chairman, Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC).Amazon India said the number of first-time jewellery shoppers rose more than 20% from the comparable festive period last year, with growth exceeding 40% in smaller cities. Flipkart Minutes said orders for gold coins and bars more than doubled in the run-up to Dhanteras. Quick commerce accounted for 80% of Bigbasket's coin orders, with one-gram gold coins the most popular.Auto companies also enjoyed strong demand. "We are expecting to deliver around 30,000 vehicles on Dhanteras this year," said Partho Banerjee, senior executive officer for marketing and sales at Maruti Suzuki India. The estimate is lower than the 41,000 deliveries Maruti reported in 2025 as Dhanteras was spread over two days. This festival season -- from Ganesh Chaturthi in Sept to Nov 6 -- the country's largest carmaker has sold 4 lakh vehicles compared with a little under 3.5 lakh last year.Hyundai Motor India's estimate covered both Dhanteras and Diwali. "We expect to deliver around 16,000 units, nearly 14% higher than last year," said MD and CEO Tarun Garg."Dhanteras saw an outstanding response, with single-day deliveries expected to cross 12,000 vehicles," said Amit Kamat, chief commercial officer at Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles.Mahindra & Mahindra said it was operating at full capacity, with physical dealer stocks close to zero across most of its SUV range. Rajesh Jejurikar, executive director and CEO of its auto and farm sector, said the company was sticking to its outlook of mid-to-high-teen SUV growth in FY27.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mortgage rates drop and stocks rebound slightly
articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Business & Economy newsletter {beacon} Business & Economy The Big Story Mortgage rates drop and stocks rebound slightly Mortgage rates declined for the third straight week, while stocks rallied on Friday after multiple days of losses this week. © Seth Wenig, Associated Press The average 30-year mortgage rate was 7.18…
articles.body:
Mortgage rates drop and stocks rebound slightly

Mortgage rates declined for the third straight week , while stocks rallied on Friday after multiple days of losses this week.

The average 30-year mortgage rate was 7.18 percent this week, Freddie Mac reported Thursday. That marked a decline of 6 basis points from last week, with 1 basis point reflecting 0.01 percent.

The average 30-year mortgage rate has declined for three straight weeks, after hitting 7.4 percent in October. Mortgage rates have spiked amid rising bond yields and oil prices.

The average 15-year mortgage rate also declined, from 6.6 percent last week to 6.57 percent this week , Freddie Mac reported. The average 15-year rate, which homeowners typically reach for when they refinance, has declined for four consecutive weeks.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite also rallied Friday after the market endured heavy losses during Thursday’s session. The indices closed the day up 23 points and up 264 points , respectively.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, though, finished the week down 237 points from closing time on Thursday. The Dow dipped by more than 700 points from Monday’s opening bell.

Stocks tanked on Thursday amid a wave of investors selling tech shares, as concerns mount over AI-related debt tech companies have racked up.

While mortgage rates declined and two major indices rose on Friday, Americans remained concerned about affordability — a major reason for Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories this week.

Democratic lawmakers and candidates campaigned on lowering the cost of living , as Americans face elevated gas prices due to the Iran war and persistently high grocery and healthcare costs.

Greater than 40 percent of voters told NBC News their family’s financial situation had gotten worse in the past two years , while 38 percent said it had stayed the same and 18 percent said it had gotten better.

Welcome to The Hill’s Business & Economy newsletter , I’m Max Rego — covering the intersection of Wall Street and Pennsylvania Avenue.

articles.title: US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
articles.summary: Trump-Xi Busan deal aimed to ease tariffs and tech restrictions; progress hinges on China’s fulfilment of commitments.
articles.body:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to urge Beijing to immediately implement commitments under the Busan trade agreement.

“Secretary Bessent emphasised the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments made in Busan and raised concerns about recent Chinese actions. He underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement,” the US Department of the Treasury said in a statement announcing the discussions on Friday.

The announcement refers to a trade deal negotiated between Washington and Beijing in which US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to ease tariffs and lift restrictions on tech to de-escalate tensions amid tit-for-tat tariffs imposed first by Washington and then by Beijing.

On Thursday, China said it was open to buying more US farm goods if the world’s two largest economies agreed to implement the reciprocal tariff cut.

“China has consistently been open to expanding purchases of agricultural products from the US, but only on the condition that the two sides implement their agreed ’30 billion for 30 billion’ reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement,” Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson Huang Ling said in a statement.

The move follows a September meeting between Trump and Xi, when the White House proposed $60bn in cuts, including $17bn worth of US farm goods.

In May, the White House said Beijing agreed to buy $17bn of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year’s target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made last October to buy US soya beans.

“Secretary Bessent reiterated the Trump Administration’s commitment to pursuing trade and economic policies that benefit American workers, farmers, and businesses and strengthen U.S. economic and national security,” the Treasury added.

articles.title: Pollution drives sales of air purifiers
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Sales of air purifiers are witnessing a sharp jump as pollution levels worsen across the country, even as the onset of winter spurs demand for
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Sales of air purifiers are witnessing a sharp jump as pollution levels worsen across the country, even as the onset of winter spurs demand for other seasonal appliances including room heaters, geysers and electric kettles. Air-purifier sales on Amazon doubled over the past week alone, while those across e-commerce platforms grew 1.4 times in Sept-Oct compared with the same period last year.Quick-commerce platforms, including Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart too, are seeing a sharp rise in demand, with consumers in Tier 2 cities adding to the growth momentum, analysts and industry experts told TOI.Daily sales of winter appliances on Q-commerce touched Rs 29 lakh in Oct, up 55% from Sept and 50% over Oct last year. Air purifiers led the month-on-month surge, with daily sales jumping 3.7x to Rs 9.6 lakh, while room-heater sales rose 1.6x to nearly Rs 10 lakh, data culled from 1DigitalStack, a market intelligence platform, said.The trend points to an early start to the seasonal buying cycle, with online sales expected to scale up further as temperatures dip. Typically, about 3 in 10 winter appliance sales are registered online."We are projecting a robust 31% year-on-year growth for the winter appliance category - specifically geysers, room heaters and electric kettles across e-commerce platforms. This season's surge is heavily catalyzed by the flagship annual festive sales on Amazon and Flipkart marketplaces, which have shifted consumer behaviour towards front-loading their winter utility purchases to maximise discounts,'' Samiran Mathur, VP insights and strategy at 1DigitalStack said.The current demand in these appliances is just a fraction of the expected peak. Last year, the quick commerce winter appliance market multiplied 5.7x from Oct to Nov, eventually hitting a Jan peak that was nearly 10x the Oct baseline, the data said. "With the onset of winters, we are seeing air-purifier sales on Amazon.in growing 2x in the last week. Customers are using Rufus, our personalised AI shopping assistant, to find the right fit. To serve immediate needs, we have expanded our air purifier selection on Amazon Now," an Amazon India spokesperson said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Electronics and IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw called on social media platforms to take greater responsibility for the content they carry,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Electronics and IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw called on social media platforms to take greater responsibility for the content they carry, pressing them to explain how their algorithms work, protect children from harmful content and give users a better way to resolve complaints.Asked whether govt was considering withdrawing safe-harbour protection for social media companies, Vaishnaw left the question open. He said the internet had changed and platforms needed to act proactively on child safety, women's safety and scams such as digital arrests, in which fraudsters pose as law enforcement officers."Throughout the Parliament debates, we have maintained that social media should take responsibility for the content. They must take all the steps that are necessary for child safety," he said.Vaishnaw linked child safety to what platforms show young users. He called for greater transparency about the algorithms that recommend content and said platforms should ensure children see material appropriate for them. He said the issue had implications for both their mental and physical health.The minister also questioned the options available to users when content on a platform causes serious harm. He said users often have little recourse beyond approaching the police or going to court and called for a more effective way for them to raise grievances and get them addressed.Vaishnaw said govt had repeatedly raised these concerns with social media companies. articles.title: US-China agree to continue trade talks as Washington presses Beijing to fulfil Busan deal commitments
articles.summary: China and the US have agreed to continue consultations to ensure stable and positive trade relations, local media Xinhua reported.
articles.body: China and the US have agreed to continue consultations to ensure stable and positive trade relations, local media Xinhua reported.The development comes as Washington pushes Beijing to fulfil the commitments made under the trade truce agreed between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Busan last year.The US has raised concerns that China is falling short of its promises on rare earth supplies, critical minerals and agricultural purchases.These concerns were discussed during a phone call on Friday morning between US treasury secretary Scott Bessent, US trade representative Jamieson Greer and Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng, who oversees trade negotiations with Washington.During the call, the US officials told China that it needed to fully deliver on the commitments made under the Busan agreement. In a post on X on Friday, he said, “ Today, US trade representative Greer and I spoke with Vice Premier He Lifeng about the US-China economic relationship and implementation of the Busan arrangement.Bessent further raised concerns about China's recent actions. "I emphasized the importance of China fully and immediately honoring its commitments, raised concerns about recent Chinese actions and underscored that progress depends on concrete results.”One of Washington's biggest concerns is China's supply of rare earths. US officials told the FT in September that China was meeting only about two-thirds of its commitments on rare earths under the Busan agreement.A person familiar with the matter said Beijing had not increased supplies even after Bessent raised the issue directly with He in New York in September, ahead of Xi's meeting with Trump in Washington.China has rejected the US claims that it is not meeting its promises on rare earth supplies.The two countries also differ over agricultural purchases. The US believes China has met its commitment to buy soyabeans but has not fulfilled its promises on other agricultural products.Washington is also concerned about China's restrictions on exports of yttrium to Japan. The rare earth is used in products ranging from jet engines to missiles. Japan makes components for products manufactured in the US, and Japanese companies have warned their government that their stockpiles of yttrium are running dangerously low.The Busan trade truce was agreed in October 2025 and was originally due to expire on January 10. However, during Xi's visit to Washington in September, the two countries extended the deadline by two months, until January 2027, after negotiators failed to resolve their differences.You use AI every day. articles.body: MUMBAI: RBI has proposed tighter rules for classifying gold-backed farm loans as priority sector lending (PSL), requiring banks to verify borrowers' actual agricultural credit needs against the district scale of finance for the crop. Banks would also have to document field inspections, crop hypothecation and evidence of agricultural activity by landless cultivators failing which loans will be classified as the more expensive gold loans.Under RBI's consolidated priority sector instructions, the draft of which was released on Thursday, a major proposal would prevent banks from excluding trade bills discounted under letters of credit from adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) when calculating PSL obligations. While such exposures can be treated as interbank credit for capital adequacy and the Large Exposure Framework, the underlying credit goes to the constituent borrower and qualifies as domestic bank credit under Form A of the RBI Act. The draft would restrict interbank treatment to capital adequacy calculations.The change could raise banks' lending obligations. Every Rs 10,000 crore of discounted bills retained in ANBC would increase the 40% PSL requirement by Rs 4,000 crore. The additional obligations would include Rs 1,800 crore for agriculture, Rs 1,400 crore for non-corporate farmers, Rs 1,000 crore for small and marginal farmers, Rs 750 crore for micro-enterprises and Rs 1,200 crore for weaker sections. The farmer sub-targets overlap with the overall agricultural target.Corporate banks could face a compliance gap because bills discounted for conglomerates, infrastructure contractors and wholesale vendors would expand the ANBC denominator without adding eligible PSL assets.Only bills involving qualifying borrowers, such as MSME suppliers, would contribute to PSL achievement. Banks may therefore need additional rural lending or PSLC purchases.The financial burden could be significant for corporate bill discounting, which typically earns spreads of 50-90 basis points. Banks may have to buy PSLCs at 80-120 basis points or place funds with development finance institutions at 200-400 basis points below the Bank Rate.
